title: The Key That Never Comes Round Again: a Secretary Among the Alphabets
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Bourbonnais Boy and the Schools of Paris

stops.name: Saint-Pourçain-sur-Sioule, birth on the Sioule
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the accepted scholarly date, carried identically by English and French Wikipedia and by the BnF authority record. No contemporary baptismal register was located in any source consulted, so the day is agreed rather than documented.
stops.campa: A son is born at Saint-Pourçain-sur-Sioule, a wine town on the river in the Bourbonnais, and is carried for baptism to Sainte-Croix, the old priory church that serves the parish and stands at the centre of the place. The boy is Blaise de Vigenère. No register survives to fix the day. The date comes down through the biographers, who all give the fifth of April 1523, and the authority records at the BnF repeat it after them. Not one of them cites a document.
suggested_refs: The église Sainte-Croix at Saint-Pourçain-sur-Sioule, former priory and parish church of his birthplace

stops.name: Paris, sent up at twelve
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact, approximate as to the year; the sources give his age, about twelve, rather than a date, and the month and day here are defaults.
stops.campa: His father sends him up to Paris at about twelve, out of the Bourbonnais and into the Latin Quarter, for the classical education a provincial gentleman's son needs if he means to serve. He is young enough to take the language of the schools the way a native takes speech, and he never afterward loses the accent of it. The city he enters is the Paris of the royal readers and of the printing houses of the rue Saint-Jacques, with Greek arriving faster than the schools can absorb it. The sources give his age, not the year.
suggested_refs: The Latin Quarter schools of the 1530s, before the Collège Royal had premises of its own

stops.name: Paris, three years and no degree
stops.date_confidence: attested for the enrolment and the rough duration; month and day are defaults. Contradiction flagged and not resolved: some reference infoboxes name the Collège de Coqueret as his school, but Jean Dorat became principal there only around 1547 and Adrien Turnèbe became royal reader in Greek in 1547, so the Coqueret-Turnèbe-Dorat combination cannot belong to his teens.
stops.campa: At about fourteen he is entered at the University of Paris. He stays roughly three years and leaves with no degree recorded anywhere, which in his century is unremarkable: a degree is for men who mean to teach or to plead, and he means to serve. What he carries away is Latin good enough to bring over Caesar and Livy fifty years later, and a reading habit no employer will ever entirely absorb. Which college housed him is not established, and the names usually attached to it belong to a later decade of his life.
suggested_refs: French Wikipedia, 'Collège de Coqueret', whose own article never mentions Vigenère

stops.name: Paris, the desk of Gilbert Bayard
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the employer; month and day are defaults. The address of Bayard's Paris household is not established, so the coordinate is the canonical Paris pin, not a landmark.
stops.campa: He enters the household of Gilbert Bayard, first secretary to Francis I, and learns the trade he will practise for thirty years: the drafting of letters, the keeping of registers, the discretion of a man who handles paper other men must not read. Nobody sets out to teach him cryptography. A royal secretary in 1539 already works with cipher as a matter of routine, because the crown's correspondence with its envoys travels through country that is not friendly. Vigenère is sixteen years old when he starts.
suggested_refs: The secretarial apparatus of the French crown under Francis I: registers, chiffres, and couriers

stops.name: Worms, the Diet and the junior secretary
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the mission; month and day are defaults. The coordinate is Worms Cathedral, the emblematic landmark of the city; the Reichstag of 1545 sat in the town, not under the cathedral vaults, and no claim is made that he entered it.
stops.campa: He crosses into the Empire as junior secretary to Louis Adhémar de Monteil, comte de Grignan, the French envoy to the Diet sitting at Worms. The cathedral is the landmark of the city, but the estates sit in the town and not under its vaults, and nothing consulted here puts him inside either building. The Diet is attempting, and failing, to settle the religious quarrel that will break open as the Schmalkaldic War within two years, and a junior secretary sees the failure from inside the delegation's own papers. He is twenty-two.
suggested_refs: The Reichstag of Worms, 1545, and the negotiations preceding the Schmalkaldic War

stops.name: Holland, the two years with no record
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. French Wikipedia says only Germany and Holland until 1547, with no town, patron, or itinerary; the coordinate is a placeholder for a documented gap, not a verified stop, and stands for Holland because that is the word the source uses.
stops.campa: After Worms he does not come straight home. The French tradition says Germany and Holland until 1547 and gives no town, no patron, no correspondent, no date inside those two years. He is somewhere in the Low Countries in his early twenties, in Habsburg territory, at exactly the moment the war he watched the Diet fail to prevent is being fought. The record resumes when he takes a post back in France. Who paid him, where he lodged, whether he was working at all: no source reached here answers.
suggested_refs: The Habsburg Netherlands in the mid-1540s, through which his route is presumed to run

segments.name: The House of Nevers and the First Rome

stops.name: Nevers, secretary to the duke
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year by both English and French Wikipedia; month and day are defaults. Whether he was regularly resident at the ducal seat or travelled with the household is not established, and the palace article does not name François Ier de Clèves as resident there.
stops.campa: Francis I dies in the spring, and Vigenère, twenty-four, enters the service of François Ier de Clèves, duke of Nevers, as secretary. It is the tie that holds for the rest of his life and outlasts three dukes of the house. He has moved, in eight years, from a first secretary's household to a sovereign duke's, and he is still nobody's principal. The ducal palace above the Loire is the seat of the house. Whether he was regularly resident there or travelled with the household, the sources do not say.
suggested_refs: The Palais ducal de Nevers, seat of the house of Clèves

stops.name: Rome, among the marbles
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sojourn; sources differ on its length, English Wikipedia giving three to four years and French Wikipedia two. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: He goes to Italy for the first time and settles in Rome, two years by one account and three or four by another. He works the ruins the way a secretary works an archive: the marble reliefs, the bronzes, the coins, the medals, the cut cameos, and the antiquarians who can read them. To bring back a vanished world from the marks it left is decipherment carried out on stone. Writing the years up thirty years later, in the middle of his book about ciphers, he says he could restore nothing.
stops.quote: in Rome, I did all that was possible - talking to learned men versed in Roman antiquity, visiting and revisiting the marble reliefs, bronzes, medals and ancient cameos from which one might draw knowledge and instruction - but I couldn't restore anything.
stops.quote_source: Blaise de Vigenère, Traicté des chiffres (1586), trans. Margaret M. McGowan (2000), p. 107, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Blaise de Vigenère'
suggested_refs: The Roman Forum and the antiquarian circles of mid-century Rome
sources: Margaret M. McGowan, The Vision of Rome in Late Renaissance France (2000)

stops.name: Venice, a stop the sources cannot date
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a live contradiction left standing: two independent readings of the same English Wikipedia article place the Venice visit on opposite sides of a seventeen-year gap, either the first Roman residence of about 1549 to 1553 or the embassy years 1566 to 1569. The date here orders the segment and is not a finding.
stops.campa: Later accounts put him in Venice on one of his two Italian residences. They do not agree which. Two readings of the same encyclopedia article, fetched separately, assign the Venetian and Florentine visits to different decades of his life, and nothing in either fixes a year, a patron, or a piece of business. Venice in either decade is the European capital of the ciphered dispatch, its chancery secretaries the most practised in Christendom at the work he will spend his life describing.
suggested_refs: The Venetian chancery and its sixteenth-century cipher secretaries

stops.name: Florence, the same uncertainty
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, weakly attested. Named among his Italian stops in later biographical accounts without a fixable year; the same unresolved dating contradiction as the Venice stop. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Florence carries the same uncertainty as Venice and rests on the same thin line in the same article. It is named among his Italian stops, with no year that can be assigned to one residence rather than the other, and with no business, patron, or correspondent attached to it. A Frenchman of his trade in Florence would have gone to the Medici collections and to the antiquarians who kept them, which is what he did in Rome; the sources do not say that he went, only that he was there. The Roman evidence is strong and this is not. It stands here because striking it would make the record tidier than the record is.
suggested_refs: Florentine antiquarian collections of the mid-sixteenth century

stops.name: Nevers, the line ends and the study reopens
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death of François II de Clèves in 1562 and for the resumption of study after it; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: François Ier de Clèves is already dead; in 1562 his son François II dies in turn, and the direct male line of the dukes of Nevers ends. Vigenère is thirty-nine, a career secretary whose house has lost its head twice in two years, in a kingdom sliding into its first religious war. He does not look for a new master. He goes back to school instead, to Greek and to Hebrew, and gives the next decade to two languages nobody is going to pay him to know. Everything printed under his name comes out of these years, and nothing out of the thirty that preceded them. He is thirty-nine years old and begins again.
suggested_refs: The extinction of the direct Clèves line at Nevers, 1562

segments.name: Going Back to School at Thirty-Nine

stops.name: Paris, Turnèbe in a borrowed hall
stops.date_confidence: attested for the association, bounded by hard dates on Turnèbe's side: royal reader in Greek from 1547, moved to Greek philosophy in 1562, died 12 June 1565. The window is therefore 1562 to 1565 at most. Anachronism flagged: the Collège Royal had no building of its own in Vigenère's lifetime, and the coordinate marks the later Collège de France site.
stops.campa: He attaches himself to Adrien Turnèbe, royal reader and the finest Greek scholar in France. The association cannot be long: Turnèbe leaves the Greek chair for Greek philosophy in 1562 and dies of consumption on the twelfth of June 1565, three years at the outside. The Collège Royal has no premises of its own and will not have any until 1610, so the teaching happens in whatever hall can be borrowed for the hour: a room, a lectern, a royal reader construing Greek aloud to whoever has come in off the street.
suggested_refs: The royal readers of the Collège Royal, lecturing without a building before 1610

stops.name: Paris, Dorat and the layered reading
stops.date_confidence: attested as an association; the strength of the teacher relation varies across sources, some calling Dorat his master and others recording only contact. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Jean Dorat, principal of Coqueret and master of the poets who call themselves the Pléiade, is the second name attached to Vigenère's Greek. Dorat's method is to read a Greek text aloud and open it outward into allegory, layer beneath layer, until a poem has become a cosmology. Vigenère will annotate exactly that way for the rest of his life, at ruinous length. How formal the relation was the sources will not settle. Some call Dorat his master; others record only that the two men were in contact.
suggested_refs: Jean Dorat's allegorical method of Greek exposition and its effect on French annotation

stops.name: Paris, Hebrew with Gilbert Génébrard
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact of study; no Paris address, abbey, or college for the lessons was located, so the coordinate is the canonical Paris pin. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: For Hebrew he goes to Gilbert Génébrard, the Benedictine Hebraist and future archbishop of Aix, one of the few men in Paris able to take a Frenchman through the rabbinic commentators. The alphabet he learns here is not only a language. It is a system in which every letter carries a number and a name, and in which permutation is a recognized operation performed on a sacred text rather than a trick played on an ordinary one. Where in Paris the lessons happened, nothing records.
suggested_refs: Gilbert Génébrard's Hebrew teaching in Paris and his later archbishopric of Aix

stops.name: Paris, La Boderie and the Christian Kabbalah
stops.date_confidence: attested for the association; no specific location located, coordinate is the canonical Paris pin. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Guy Le Fèvre de La Boderie, who worked on the Antwerp Polyglot and put the Christian Kabbalists into French, belongs to the same Paris circle and the same formation. Where the two men met, how often, and in what year, nothing consulted here records. Through him Vigenère enters the current that reads the Hebrew letters as working parts of creation rather than as writing about it, and twenty-one years later tables of Hebrew permutation will stand in the middle of a book that court secretaries buy for its ciphers.
suggested_refs: Guy Le Fèvre de La Boderie and the Antwerp Polyglot milieu of Christian Hebraism

segments.name: The Embassy at Rome: Ciphers and a Polish Crown

stops.name: Rome, secretary to the ambassador
stops.date_confidence: attested for the mission and the year. The ambassador is better given as Just II de Tournon, ambassador 1566-1568 per the French list of ambassadors to the Holy See, succeeded by Charles d'Angennes in 1568; Vigenère's stay of about three years therefore outlasts Tournon's embassy. Coordinate is the canonical Rome city pin: no sixteenth-century French ambassadorial residence in Rome is documented, and the Palazzo Farnese only serves from 1635.
stops.campa: Catherine de Médicis and Charles IX send him back to Rome, this time as secretary to the French embassy under the ambassador Just II de Tournon. He is forty-three and is nobody's apprentice now. The embassy is a listening post: French policy in Italy runs on what the ambassador's household can learn from the papal court, from the Spanish, from the Venetians, from couriers passing through, and on how much of it can be sent home without Spain reading it on the road.
suggested_refs: French Wikipedia, 'Liste des ambassadeurs de France près le Saint-Siège', for the Tournon embassy 1566-1568
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Liste des ambassadeurs de France près le Saint-Siège'

stops.name: Rome, the Polish overture tested by mouth
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from a dossier synthesis of Catherine de Médicis's December 1566 correspondence with Tournon, cross-checked only against the confirmed 1566 embassy dates. The instruction itself was not independently verified in the sources reached.
stops.campa: In December the queen mother writes to Tournon about an approach made in Rome by a secretary of Sigismund II Augustus of Poland, hinting that the Polish crown might be brought to her son Henri, duke of Anjou. Vigenère is to sound the man out by word of mouth, establish whether the offer is real, and on no account let it be known he was told to. It is the one episode where the paper shows him working as an intelligencer and not as a clerk. The instruction itself survives only in a synthesis of Catherine's correspondence. The original was not located.
suggested_refs: The correspondence of Catherine de Médicis with the French embassy at Rome, December 1566
sources: Dossier synthesis of Catherine de Médicis's 1566 correspondence, uncorroborated elsewhere

stops.name: Rome, the Italian art of secret writing
stops.date_confidence: attested that he studied ciphers in Italy; the residence to which it belongs is narrowed here to 1566-1569 rather than the first sojourn, because Della Porta's De furtivis literarum notis was printed in 1563, after the earlier trip had ended. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: At the papal court he finds the Italian art of secret writing at its full growth: nomenclators, secret alphabets, the cipher disk Leon Battista Alberti described a hundred years before, the keyword tables Giovan Battista Bellaso printed in 1553, and the new book of Giovanni Battista Della Porta, printed in 1563 and therefore not yet in existence on his first Roman stay. The French chanceries are behind the Italians. He reads everything they have.
suggested_refs: Giovanni Battista Della Porta, De furtivis literarum notis (Naples, 1563)
Giovan Battista Bellaso, La cifra del Sig. Giovan Battista Bellaso (1553)

stops.name: Rome, the key that eats the message
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The autokey idea is conventionally dated to the second Roman residence, around 1567 to 1568, on the strength of the embassy dates and the composition history of the 1586 treatise. No dated document fixes the idea's formation to these years; the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Every Italian system repeats its key. A short word is written over and over above the message, and the repetition is the flaw, because the same key letters keep falling on the same plain letters at fixed intervals and the pattern comes through. Vigenère's move is to stop repeating. After one agreed letter, the message enciphers itself, each letter of the plain text serving as the key for the letter after it, so the key is exactly as long as the message and never comes round again.
suggested_refs: The plaintext autokey as described in the Traicté des chiffres, 1586

stops.name: Paris, married at forty-seven
stops.date_confidence: attested; both English and French Wikipedia give the same date. No parish church for the marriage was located, so the coordinate is the canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of July, at forty-seven, he marries Marie Varé in Paris and stops travelling. The itinerant half of the life closes here: no more embassies, no more Roman winters, no more crossing into the Empire behind an envoy. What follows is twenty-six years at a desk in one city, and it is the productive part of the life by a wide margin. Almost everything anyone now knows him for is written after this wedding. The bride's family, her dowry, and the household they set up are not described in any source consulted here; Marie Varé enters the record on her wedding day and does not appear in it again.
suggested_refs: Parisian marriage records of 1570, in which no act for Vigenère and Marie Varé was located

stops.name: Paris, the thousand livres given away
stops.date_confidence: biographical tradition, tagged generously in the sources. Both encyclopedias repeat it without a charitable register or a notarial act; French Wikipedia has him offering the annual pension to the poor of Paris, English Wikipedia has him donating the income, and neither limits it to the first year. Month and day here are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He retires on a pension of a thousand livres a year and gives it to the poor of Paris. Both encyclopedias carry the story in the same words and neither cites a register, an act, or a witness who saw it done. He had married into money and could afford the gesture, and it is exactly the sort of gesture biographers keep and repeat until it hardens. The two articles do not even agree in shape: one has him handing over the pension itself, the other the income from it. Whether it was done once, or every year, or at all, no source reached here can show.
suggested_refs: Parisian charitable registers of the 1570s, not located or consulted

stops.name: Paris, secretary of the King's Chamber
stops.date_confidence: attested for the title, held under Henri III and printed on his title pages; the year of the grant is not fixed in the sources and this date orders the segment. Coordinate is the Louvre, the court's Paris seat, not a documented office of his.
stops.campa: He takes the title secretary of the King's Chamber under Henri III and prints it on his title pages, where it does the work a title-page title exists to do: it tells a buyer that the man annotating Livy is employed by the crown. The office belongs to the court, and in these years the court is at the Louvre. He has spent his working life writing other men's words down for them, and from here he writes his own. The labour is done at home, over folio sheets, in a hand trained since he was sixteen to be legible to strangers.
suggested_refs: The title 'secretaire de la chambre du Roy' as printed on Vigenère's imprints

stops.name: Paris, the Polish books for a French prince
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the printer, Jean Richer, Paris 1573, for both Polish titles. Coordinate corrected to the Latin Quarter, rue Saint-Jean-de-Latran, where Richer's shop stood; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Henri of Anjou is standing for the elective crown of Poland, and France needs telling what Poland is. Seven years earlier Vigenère had been sent to find out quietly whether that crown was in play; now he explains the kingdom to its new king's French subjects in print. He supplies the Chroniques et annales de Poloigne and the Description du royaume de Poloigne, both printed by Jean Richer in 1573, compiled out of other men's books. He has never set foot in the country.
suggested_refs: Jean Richer's shop in the rue Saint-Jean-de-Latran, near the Collège Royal

stops.name: Paris, the entry at Mantua written up
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication, 1576. His personal presence at the 1574 entry at Mantua is NOT established by any source consulted, so no Mantua stop is made: the book is placed at its Paris imprint. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Henri abandons Cracow, rides west for the French crown, and is received at Mantua by the Gonzaga on the road. Vigenère writes the account of that entry and it is printed at Paris in 1576, a festival book of the sort the century consumes eagerly. Festival books of this kind are often assembled in a capital, out of relations and dispatches, by men who never left it. Did he stand in the street and watch the arches and the Gonzaga liveries go past, or did he work the whole thing up from paper in Paris? Nothing consulted here can say.
suggested_refs: La somptueuse et magnifique entrée du roi Henri III à Mantoue (Paris, 1576)

stops.name: Paris, the decline of the Greeks
stops.date_confidence: attested; the imprint is Paris, Nicolas Chesneau, 1577, confirmed independently by the BnF catalogue and musicologie.org. Coordinate corrected to the rue Saint-Jacques, at the sign of the green oak, where Chesneau's shop stood.
stops.campa: Nicolas Chesneau prints, at the sign of the green oak in the rue Saint-Jacques, Vigenère's French Laonikos Chalkokondyles: the history of the decline of the Greek empire and of the establishment of that of the Turks. He is fifty-four and has found the form that fits him, which is neither translation nor commentary but a Greek historian carried over into French and then buried under a Frenchman's reading of him. The annotation runs longer than the text it annotates.
suggested_refs: L'Histoire de la décadence de l'Empire grec et establissement de celuy des Turcs (Paris, N. Chesneau, 1577)

stops.name: Paris, the painted tablets of Philostratus
stops.date_confidence: attested by musicologie.org, which gives Paris, Nicolas Chesneau, 1578, for the first edition; noted because the English Wikipedia works list omits the 1578 edition and shows only the enlarged 1597 L'Angelier printing. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: The same printer brings out Les images ou tableaux de platte peinture de Philostrate lemnien: sixty-five ancient paintings described in Greek prose by a writer who may have been describing pictures that never hung anywhere. Vigenère turns each description into an essay of his own, so that a paragraph of Greek about a boy and a river becomes twenty pages on rivers, boys, and painting. Of everything he wrote, this is the book that lasts: reissued through the following century, and put into English by a scholarly press as late as 1976.
suggested_refs: Les images ou tableaux de platte peinture de Philostrate lemnien (Paris, N. Chesneau, 1578)

stops.name: Paris, the hairy star
stops.date_confidence: attested for the comet of 1577 and for the treatise printed in 1578; the month here orders the sequence within the year. Coordinate is the canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: A comet hangs over Europe through the winter and is watched from Paris. Vigenère writes the Traicté des comètes, ou estoilles chevelues and prints it the following year, setting the ancient authorities beside what observers report and reading the object as a sign sent. He is not being credulous by the standard of 1578. Astrology, ancient authority, and what men actually saw in the sky share one book without embarrassment, because they are not yet separate inquiries.
suggested_refs: The great comet of 1577 and its European literature

segments.name: The Translator's Decade and the Traicté des Chiffres

stops.name: Paris, Caesar carried into French
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1582 publication of the annotated Caesar, with an expanded edition in 1589; month and day are defaults. Coordinate is Abel L'Angelier's shop in the Galerie du Palais.
stops.campa: Abel L'Angelier prints his Julius Caesar, the Commentaries in French with annotation heavy enough to double the volume. Vigenère is translating a general who, on Suetonius's testimony, wrote to Oppius and to Balbus in a cipher that shifted every letter three places along the alphabet: the oldest named cipher in the Latin record, passing through the hands of the man who is four years from writing the century's largest book about ciphers. An expanded edition follows in 1589.
suggested_refs: Suetonius on Caesar's shifted alphabet in the letters to Oppius and Balbus
julius_caesar.journey.json, the Bibracte stop for the substitution cipher

stops.name: Paris, the Decades of Livy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, consistent with the documented chronology of his 1580s classical translations; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Livy follows, the Decades in French, with antiquarian notes, images, and a chronology laid alongside. He is sixty and running a one-man translation programme out of a Paris house: the Greeks, the Romans, the Byzantines, the crusaders, each brought over and then smothered in learning. L'Angelier at the Galerie du Palais can sell it, because a French reader who wants Livy in 1583 has very few other doors to knock at. The kingdom outside the shop is in the middle of its wars of religion. Inside it, an old secretary is establishing the chronology of the Roman republic to the year.
suggested_refs: Abel L'Angelier's shop in the Galerie du Palais, Paris

stops.name: Paris, Villehardouin in two columns
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the parallel-text form; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: He prints Geoffroi de Villehardouin's account of the taking of Constantinople with the old French standing in one column and his own modernized version beside it. He does not replace the thirteenth-century language, he exhibits it, and lets a reader watch what four hundred years have done to the words. A man who spends his life on alphabets is treating his own tongue as something that needs a key. It is a small editorial decision, and an unusual one for the century.
suggested_refs: L'Histoire de Geoffroy de Villehardouin, in parallel old and modern French (Paris, 1585)

stops.name: Paris, the Traicté des chiffres
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, the printer Abel L'Angelier, and the place; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Abel L'Angelier prints the Traicté des chiffres, ou Secretes manieres d'escrire, six hundred folios on scripts, ciphers, alphabets, numbers, and the philosophy of signs. Secret writing here is not a technique but an account of what writing is, which is why Hebrew letters, Chinese characters, and hieroglyphs stand in the same volume as Alberti, Bellaso, and Della Porta. The tabula recta that Johannes Trithemius put into print in 1518, the square of shifted alphabets, is in it too.
suggested_refs: Johannes Trithemius, Polygraphia (Oppenheim, 1518), source of the tabula recta
johannes_trithemius.journey.json, the 1518 Oppenheim printing

stops.name: Paris, the autokey shown at court
stops.date_confidence: attested that the plaintext autokey is described in the 1586 treatise and was presented before the court of Henri III; the month orders the sequence within the year of publication.
stops.campa: Inside the treatise, and presented before the court of Henri III, stands the cipher that is genuinely his: the plain text used as its own key, one agreed letter to start it, no repetition anywhere along the message. It is stronger than anything the Italians have printed. It is also not the system that will carry his name. What posterity calls the Vigenère cipher is Bellaso's repeating keyword of 1553, which this same book prints, and which is the weaker of the two.
suggested_refs: The plaintext-autokey chapter of the Traicté des chiffres
David Kahn, The Codebreakers, on the Bellaso misattribution

stops.name: Paris, the permutation tables inside the book
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Hebrew permutation tables are in the 1586 treatise; the month orders the sequence. The modern decipherment of how the tables run is by the ethnologist David Rouach in 1989, in his book Les Talismans: Magie et traditions juives, not a scholarly edition of Vigenère.
stops.campa: Buried in the same volume are tables of Hebrew letter permutation, tserouf, the operation the kabbalists perform on the letters of scripture so the text will yield what is folded into it. They are not decoration. A secretary enciphering a dispatch and a kabbalist permuting the divine name are doing, on Vigenère's account, the same thing to the same material, and the book is arranged so that a reader cannot take the one without the other. Buyers take the ciphers. It is 1989 before anyone works out how his Hebrew tables actually run.
suggested_refs: David Rouach, Les Talismans: Magie et traditions juives (1989), where the operating key of Vigenère's tserouf table is worked out

stops.name: Paris, the Psalter in measured prose
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the title; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Le Psaultier de David torné en prose mesurée, ou vers libres: the Psalms put into a French that is neither verse nor ordinary prose but a measured line, an attempt to make the language answer the rhythm of Hebrew poetry instead of forcing that poetry into rhyme. He is sixty-five, and he has been inside Hebrew long enough to hear what the rhymed psalters everyone sings have flattened out of it. The rhymed psalters are not displaced. French waits three centuries for its next serious attempt at a line without rhyme or metre.
suggested_refs: Le Psaultier de David torné en prose mesurée, ou vers libres (Paris, 1588)

segments.name: Fire, Salt, and the Grave at Saint-Étienne-du-Mont

stops.name: Paris, still the house of Nevers's man
stops.date_confidence: attested: English Wikipedia's biography documents the July 1593 letter showing service to Louis de Gonzague and the tutoring of the duke's son. A research lens on this dossier wrongly downgraded it to an unverified lead; the chronology is right and the tag is [A]. The letter does not place him at Nevers, so the coordinate is his Paris residence pin.
stops.campa: A letter of July shows him still inside the orbit of the house of Nevers, serving Louis de Gonzague and acting as tutor or guide to the duke's son. He is seventy, and every account of his life has had him retired for twenty-three years. Paris in this month is besieged and hungry and about to admit a king who is changing his religion in order to enter it. The retirement, the pension, the withdrawal into books: none of it was ever quite complete. The old secretary is teaching a duke's son his letters, in a house in a starving city, for a family he first served forty-six years earlier.
suggested_refs: The July 1593 letter concerning Louis de Gonzague, duke of Nevers, and his son

stops.name: Paris, the fire and the salt
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date. The Traicté du feu et du sel was found among his papers after his death, per its own title page, so the composition is late but undated; this date orders the segment and is not attested.
stops.campa: Among the papers he leaves is a treatise on fire and salt, an alchemical natural philosophy written in the first person, the only book of his where the voice belongs to a workman rather than to a scholar. He has done the operations himself: distilling salt, weighing litharge back down into lead, watching aqua vitae thrown up out of a glass and not one drop of it fall. He does not always know what he has seen. When that happens he says so on the page and leaves the knot for somebody else.
stops.quote: Certes herein I have lost all my Latine, and know not what to say thereof, only it is gone in verity as I say: If any one would untie this knot, would indeed do me a great pleasure.
stops.quote_source: Blaise de Vigenère, A Discovrse of Fire and Salt, trans. Edward Stephens (London: Richard Cotes, 1649)
suggested_refs: A Discovrse of Fire and Salt (London, 1649), Project Gutenberg ebook 47365
sources: Blaise de Vigenère, A Discovrse of Fire and Salt (1649), Project Gutenberg 47365

stops.name: Paris, prayers out of the Zohar
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1595 Prières et oraisons and for Vigenère's own statement of its sources, quoted in the Encyclopaedia Judaica entry; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: A year before he dies he prints the Prières et oraisons, and states where the material came from. A Catholic secretary of the King's Chamber, in Paris, in 1595, publishes prayers drawn out of the Jewish mystical corpus and names the books he drew them from, probably by way of Guillaume Postel's Latin Zohar. He does not disguise the provenance and he is not obliged to give it; the naming is a choice. The Hebrew he began at thirty-nine, with a Benedictine who would end as an archbishop, is still working in him at seventy-two. It is the last thing he sees through a press.
stops.quote: mainly drawn from the Zohar, the Sefer ha-Bahir or Book of Splendor, the Midrash Tehillim, and other little-known works.
stops.quote_source: Vigenère on the sources of his Prières et oraisons (Paris, 1595), quoted in the Encyclopaedia Judaica entry 'Vigenère, Blaise de'
suggested_refs: Guillaume Postel's Latin Zohar, the probable channel for Vigenère's kabbalistic material

stops.name: Paris, death in February
stops.date_confidence: attested; English and French Wikipedia agree on the date, the place, and the traditional cause. The throat cancer is a retrospective diagnosis carried by biographical tradition, with no surviving medical record behind it.
stops.campa: He dies in Paris on the nineteenth of February, seventy-two years old. The tradition says throat cancer, a diagnosis made backward through the biographies with no medical record under it. He leaves behind, in print, Caesar and Livy and Chalkokondyles and Philostratus and Villehardouin, a treatise on comets, a psalter in measured prose, and one very large book about ciphers; and in manuscript, among the papers on the table, an account of fire and salt that nobody has seen.
suggested_refs: The traditional attribution of his death to throat cancer, unsupported by any located record

stops.name: Saint-Étienne-du-Mont, the burial
stops.date_confidence: attested for the church by French Wikipedia and encyclopedia.com; the day after the death is an ordering device, not a recorded date. Coordinate contradiction flagged: the research lenses gave 48.8462/2.3477 and 48.8462/2.3488 for the same church, and the second is used here.
stops.campa: He is buried at Saint-Étienne-du-Mont, on the slope behind the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève, a few streets from the university he left without a degree sixty years earlier. Whether the tomb survives, whether any stone or plaque inside the church names him, no source consulted here can say: the encyclopedias record the burial and record nothing after it. What the French article does note is that Blaise Pascal, born almost exactly a century after him, lies in the same church.
stops.quote: Sa tombe est à l'église Saint-Étienne-du-Mont
suggested_refs: The église Saint-Étienne-du-Mont, Paris, burial place also of Blaise Pascal

stops.name: Galerie du Palais, Philostratus enlarged
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1597 enlarged edition, Paris, Abel L'Angelier, per the English Wikipedia works list; month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Abel L'Angelier brings out the revised and enlarged Images ou tableaux de platte peinture, a year after the annotator's death. The first edition had come from Chesneau in 1578; this one carries the additions Vigenère had gone on making, and it is the book of his the seventeenth century keeps reprinting. The additions came out of papers and corrected copies left in the house, prepared for the press by other hands. What else was in that house, no inventory consulted here records.
suggested_refs: Les images ou tableaux de platte peinture, enlarged edition (Paris, Abel Langelier, 1597)

stops.name: Paris, the fire and salt printed at last
stops.date_confidence: contested and left contested. English Wikipedia's works list says first edition 1608 but gives the catalogued imprint as Paris, Abel Langelier, 1618; musicologie.org lists only Paris, Vve A. L'Angelier, 1618. Abel L'Angelier died in 1610, so an 1618 Paris printing is by his widow, and the 1608/1618 split is two imprints rather than a typographical error. Only 1618 is bibliographically attested in the sources reached, so it is used here.
stops.campa: The Traicté du feu et du sel is printed at last, its title page saying the text was found among his papers after his decease. The bibliography is not clean: one works list gives a first edition of 1608, but the imprint actually catalogued is Paris, 1618, from the widow of Abel L'Angelier, L'Angelier himself having died in 1610. Through an English translation the workman's voice survives in a language he never wrote a line of. Edward Stephens makes it, for the printer Richard Cotes, London 1649, under the title A Discovrse of Fire and Salt.
stops.quote: I have put you to an addresse of great effects, where I do not pretend to lead you by the hand any further, not to injure good and curious spirits, that by long labours and perquisitions have travelled to obtaine that which others had better cheap.
stops.quote_source: Blaise de Vigenère, A Discovrse of Fire and Salt, trans. Edward Stephens (London: Richard Cotes, 1649)
suggested_refs: Traicté du feu et du sel (Paris, Vve A. L'Angelier, 1618)
A Discovrse of Fire and Salt (London, 1649)

stops.name: Paris, the cipher that was never his
stops.date_confidence: posthumous reception, stated as such. Kasiski's Die Geheimschriften und die Dechiffrir-Kunst is attested to 1863; the stop is placed at the imprint pin of Vigenère's own book because it concerns that book's name and not any place Vigenère went. Charles Babbage's private break of 1854 belongs to Babbage's own file and is cited here only as a source.
stops.campa: A retired Prussian infantry officer, Friedrich Wilhelm Kasiski, publishes the method that breaks the repeating-keyword cipher, by measuring the intervals between strings that repeat in the ciphertext and deducing the length of the key from them. The cipher he breaks had been called indecipherable for three centuries and had been called Vigenère's for one. It is Bellaso's, printed in 1553, thirty-three years before the Traicté des chiffres. The autokey, the one that does not repeat, was never what the name was fixed to.
suggested_refs: Friedrich Kasiski, Die Geheimschriften und die Dechiffrir-Kunst (1863)

stops.name: Saint-Pourçain-sur-Sioule, the name over a schoolyard
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source: French Wikipedia states only that the cité scolaire of Saint-Pourçain-sur-Sioule bears his name, with no year of naming. The date here is purely an ordering device and should not be read as a finding.
stops.campa: In the town on the Sioule the secondary school carries his name. It is the only concrete namesake anybody has been able to locate: no statue, no street confirmed, no plaque found in the church where he was baptized or in the church where he lies. The French article gives no year for the naming. A man whose books ran to six hundred folios, who read Greek with Turnèbe and Hebrew with Génébrard, is commemorated where he was born by a signboard over a schoolyard.
stops.quote: La citée scolaire de Saint-Pourçain-sur-Sioule porte son nom.
suggested_refs: The cité scolaire Blaise de Vigenère, Saint-Pourçain-sur-Sioule
